card.hook: Picture a green ribbon rolling out in front of you, dead straight, all the way to the mountains. That's Odori Park from the top of the Sapporo TV Tower, and it's the kind of view that makes you say "huh" out loud.
card.stand_here: Go up to the observation deck of the Sapporo TV Tower (さっぽろテレビ塔) at the east end of the park and face west, along the length of the park. The middle of the park is about 835 m west of the tower.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the whole park in one shot, then switch to 1x for a cleaner look at the city grid. Try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the mountains or one flower bed.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the park up with a vertical grid line so it runs straight away from you, with a little sky and the mountains in the top third.
card.best_time: Go at dusk, when you can catch the sunset and the first street lights in the same shot. The view changes with the seasons, so winter festival structures and summer flowers each give you a different picture.
card.selfie_here: Head to the sunken rose garden at the western end of the park (West 12-chome). Few visitors come out that way, so it's a private-feeling spot for a sunset portrait with roses in soft light. Or pose in front of the dancers sculpture with the TV Tower behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the subway exit at 3 Chome, where the exit sign shows the city's name, while you stand by the sign with the TV Tower in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The TV Tower observation deck is a ticketed site, so check the official site for opening times, prices and the latest details. In winter, wear non-slip snow boots and layered warm clothing.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once from up on the deck and once from the park looking up at the tower, and see which one you'd put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: Odori Park is about 1.5 km long and splits Sapporo into its northern and southern halves. It began as a firebreak in the 1870s and is now a string of flower gardens and event grounds. The Sapporo Snow Festival and the Lilac Festival are both held here, and the TV Tower was erected in 1957.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the observation deck of the Sapporo TV Tower (さっぽろテレビ塔) at the east end of the park and face west, along the length of the park. The middle of the park is about 835 m west of the tower.

card.hook: Plot twist: this red-brick beauty wasn't built for beer at all. It started out as a sugar factory, and the outside is so photogenic you can happily skip the ticket queue.
card.stand_here: Head for the front entrance of the Sapporo Beer Museum in Sapporo Garden Park, then face the building so the red star and brick facade fill your view. The phone icon sits on the building itself, so use it to find the place and then walk to the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and the red star. Switch to 0.5x if you're close and want the whole building and chimney in one frame. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the star emblems and arched windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the walls and chimney with the vertical lines so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, which one guide recommends for photos of the outside.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main entrance, by the reception sign, with the red-brick facade and chimney behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low so the chimney makes it into the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the approach path leading to the entrance, far enough away to fit the whole building and chimney, while you stand in front of the entrance facing them.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says the roof, exterior walls and chimney were under repair from March to December 2025, so check that the chimney and facade are fully visible when you visit.
card.challenge: Find the red star emblem, put it in the top third of your frame and let the chimney rise right behind it.
card.good_to_know: The building went up in 1890 as a factory for the Sapporo Sugar Company. Sapporo Beer bought it in 1903 and turned it into a brewery, and it opened as a museum in July 1987. It's described as the only beer museum in Japan and became a Hokkaidō Heritage site in 2004.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the front entrance of the Sapporo Beer Museum in Sapporo Garden Park, then face the building so the red star and brick facade fill your view. The phone icon sits on the building itself, so use it to find the place and then walk to the front.

card.hook: Picture crab legs, glossy salmon roe and fish-shaped signboards, all lined up within a few steps of each other. Nijo Market is a row of seafood stalls in Sapporo, and almost every frame you take here has colour and a clear subject.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stall row along the L-shaped stretch of South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo), right at the phone icon on the map. Face the stalls and walk the whole row rather than stopping at the first one.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the stall displays and signs. Switch to 0.5x for the whole street and the mascot statues, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of crab, urchin and roe without leaning over the stalls.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the display you want, then drag the brightness slider down a little if the bright signs wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 10:00. Stall hours vary from shop to shop, so check before making a special trip.
card.selfie_here: Try the roadside mascot statues of the boy and girl on the market street, which are a popular photo stop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check your screen to see what's behind you before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Wide shots of the general atmosphere are usually fine, but ask permission before taking close-ups of the people working at the stalls.
card.challenge: Can you get a fish-shaped signboard and a splash of orange roe in the same frame?
card.good_to_know: The market is a row of seafood stalls along an L-shaped stretch of South 2nd Avenue. Crab, sea urchin, salmon roe and fish are laid out on display. For a quieter picture, Sōseigawa Park is nearby, and from the riverbank you can look back across the Sosei River toward the market buildings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the stall row along the L-shaped stretch of South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo), right at the phone icon on the map. Face the stalls and walk the whole row rather than stopping at the first one.

card.hook: Picture a giant whisky sign glowing over a junction while a tram rattles past underneath. That's Susukino after dark, and the sign's background keeps changing colour as you wait.
card.stand_here: Go to the 2nd-floor outdoor terrace of COCONO SUSUKINO. Take the escalator at the building's corner, beside the Nikka statue, then face the Nikka sign straight across the intersection.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the sign and the crossing lights fit together. If your phone has 2x, use it to fill the frame with the sign and lose the clutter below. Use 0.5x only when you want the whole junction and street.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sign, then slide the brightness a little darker so the neon keeps its colour instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Come after dark, when the neon is lit. A rainy evening is even better, because the wet road reflects the lights.
card.selfie_here: Use the 2nd-floor terrace at COCONO SUSUKINO. Turn on the front camera, and if your phone has 0.5x, use it. Stand with your back to the Nikka sign so it sits over your shoulder, a lot closer than the crosswalk lets you get.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the crosswalk on the Minami 4 West side of the intersection, across the street from the sign, so they can frame the whole sign with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace belongs to a shopping building, so check the official site for access times before you go. Near the road, watch the traffic and keep your phone strap round your wrist.
card.challenge: Catch a tram gliding through the lower part of your frame with the sign glowing above it. Try a Live Photo to help.
card.good_to_know: Susukino's name is usually translated as 'zebra grass field'. The district dates from 1871, when the pioneering authority for Hokkaidō first laid it out. There's a Susukino Festival each August and ice statues along the street every February, if you happen to be there then.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the 2nd-floor outdoor terrace of COCONO SUSUKINO. Take the escalator at the building's corner, beside the Nikka statue, then face the Nikka sign straight across the intersection.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing: the phone icon on the map drops you in the middle of the shrine grounds, but the gate everyone photographs is back at the park-side entrance. Walk over and you'll find a big wooden torii with tall trees all around it.
card.stand_here: Go to the large wooden torii at the park-side entrance of Hokkaido Shrine in Maruyama Park, and stand beside the central path, not on it, because that path is reserved for the gods. Face the gate so the approach leads away from it into the trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the torii framed by the trees. If you're close and the top of the gate gets chopped off, tap 0.5x and keep your phone level so the posts don't lean in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the torii in the middle, then tap the torii and slide it a little darker so the sky behind the dark wood doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds arrive. It gets busy in cherry blossom season, around New Year and during the Sapporo Festival (14 to 16 June), so early matters most then.
card.selfie_here: Try the broad, tree-lined stone stairway on the approach to the torii gate. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x to fit in more of the tall trees, and hold your phone a little higher so the forest frames you.
card.rules_and_safety: Follow any posted signs and stay respectful during prayers or ceremonies. Outdoor areas are generally fine for photos. In winter the gravel and paths can be uneven or slippery, so wear suitable footwear.
card.challenge: Get a friend walking up the stone steps toward the torii, with the trees on both sides and nobody else in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Hokkaido Shrine has stood on this site since 1871, and it was called Sapporo Shrine until 1964. A fire destroyed the building in 1974, and it was restored in 1978. The grounds cover about 180,000 square metres, so leave yourself a little extra time to walk in from the park.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the large wooden torii at the park-side entrance of Hokkaido Shrine in Maruyama Park, and stand beside the central path, not on it, because that path is reserved for the gods. Face the gate so the approach leads away from it into the trees.

card.hook: Sapporo TV Tower has been out-tallied by the high-rises around it, and that's good news for your photos. Those buildings make a great backdrop for an old tower that's still standing proud.
card.stand_here: Stand in Odori Park (大通公園), 3-chome section, by the subway exit near the tower. You'll be about 38 m from the base. Face the tower and tilt your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole 147 m tower fits, and expect the sides to lean in towards the top, which looks dramatic. For a calmer shot, walk back through the park and use zoom 1x or just a touch more. To snap the clocks, try zoom 5x if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, so the shot looks tidy and you leave a bit of sky above it.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon are good for softer light and fewer people. Dusk can also work well if the tower is lit.
card.selfie_here: Try the pedestrian bridge close to the tower, ideally at dusk when the tower's lights come on. Another popular spot is by the sculpture in the West 4th Street area of Odori Park. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the 3-chome subway exit with the city name on it, so the exit sign and the tower both fit in the frame, and you pose out towards the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is public, but the observation deck needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the tower, one dramatic and leaning from zoom 0.5x up close, and one calm and straight from further back, then pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: The tower was built in 1957 and was designed by Tachū Naitō, who also planned Tokyo Tower. Digital clocks were added about 65 m up in 1961, facing all four sides, and the observation deck sits at 90.38 m. The tower's basement connects to the Aurora Town underground shopping arcade.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Odori Park (大通公園), 3-chome section, by the subway exit near the tower. You'll be about 38 m from the base. Face the tower and tilt your phone up.

card.hook: Picture a tiny white-and-green wooden building that looks like it wandered into a business district and decided to stay. That's the Sapporo Clock Tower, and the plain glass and concrete behind it make it pop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Sapporo Clock Tower itself, where the phone icon sits, on the little photo stage right in front of the main entrance. Face the building to get the whole front, clock faces and tower straight on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on front view. If you can't fit the whole building in, switch to 0.5x, but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. From the terrace across the road, try 2x to pick out the clock face and tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with the centre line, then tap the clock face and slide it a touch darker so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be calmer around the front. The chimes ring on the hour, so arrive a few minutes early and shoot a Live Photo to catch a bit of sound and movement.
card.selfie_here: Try the raised platform on the right side of the front, near the road intersection, where people pose with the tower behind them. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the tower over your shoulder. The angle is diagonal and slightly upward, so hold the phone a little higher. The marked photo spot in the grounds works too if you hold the phone upright to fit the whole building.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to head up to the second-floor Clock Tower Photo Plaza terrace of the MN Building across the street, while you stand in front of the tower's main entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is free to photograph from public ground, but the museum inside is ticketed and has set opening days, so check the official site first, especially if you plan to use images commercially.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead centre on the gridlines with the clock face sharp, then try to catch the hourly chime in a Live Photo.
card.good_to_know: The tower was built in 1878 as the drill hall of the former Sapporo Agricultural College, which is now Hokkaido University. The clock was installed in 1881 by E. Howard & Co. of Boston and still keeps time. It's described as the oldest clock tower in Japan and is widely treated as a symbol of Sapporo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Sapporo Clock Tower itself, where the phone icon sits, on the little photo stage right in front of the main entrance. Face the building to get the whole front, clock faces and tower straight on.

Sources disagree on the best front-facing spot: one guide calls the MN Building terrace the best whole-building view, while a Japan Travel reader says the yard spot is crowded and the building opposite is better, and a LiveJapan article says the southwest corner next to the highway intersection is a classic spot. Some pages are older (LiveJapan's photos date from March 2018, and it notes a photo board is no longer available), so confirm the terrace and platform are still there. The 'designated photo spot' in the grounds is described only vaguely, so it may need a check on arrival. Opening hours and terrace hours were not confirmed by any page I read.

card.hook: You walk out of Sapporo Station and the building you just left keeps going up, and up, and up. JR Tower is one of those rare landmarks you can photograph before you've even bought a coffee.
card.stand_here: Start at JR Sapporo Station, because JR Tower is built directly above its South entrance. The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, so stand there and tilt your phone upwards.
card.zoom: Up close, zoom 0.5x is your friend for fitting the whole tower in. If you can step back a bit, switch to 1x, and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical one so the sides stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Dusk or early evening, when the sky is darker, is a good bet. Check whether the building is lit when you're there, and use night mode with your phone held very still.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt the phone up a little. Stand with the tower over your shoulder and keep your face on one side of the frame so the tall building gets its share.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly straight on a grid line, with a slice of sky above and a passer-by at the bottom to show how big it is.
card.good_to_know: JR Tower has 38 storeys, stands 173 m high and opened on 6 March 2003. It's part of a complex with the Stellar Place mall, the Daimaru department store, a cinema, offices and the JR Tower Hotel Nikko Sapporo. The observation deck, Tower Three Eight, is on the 38th floor, and the lift to it starts from the 6th floor.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at JR Sapporo Station, because JR Tower is built directly above its South entrance. The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, so stand there and tilt your phone upwards.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where the JR Tower is behind the visitor, so I returned no selfie spots and no ask-someone spot rather than guess. The pages describe the Tower's 38th-floor observatory (JR Tower Observatory T38) and its views, and the photo spots they name for other towers are not JR Tower spots. Photography is described as generally allowed for personal use at the observatory (airial.travel, sillysuitcase.com), but no page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, so rules is empty. Exterior photo spots would need a different search, such as a local photo guide to the Sapporo Station area.

card.hook: Picture a giant silver roof, 245 metres across, sitting right in front of you like a very shiny spaceship. You can't miss it, and it fills your phone screen without any effort.
card.stand_here: Walk about 10 minutes from Fukuzumi Station to Sapporo Dome, then stand on the open ground just outside the building, as near the phone icon on the map as you can get. Face the dome so the silver roof fills the frame behind you or your subject.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because up close the roof is too big to fit at 1x. Switch to 1x for photos of people with the dome behind them, or for a tighter shot of the roof's curve.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the roof's curve up with a grid line, then tap the roof and make the picture a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a day with some clear sky, because that's when the silver roof really stands out. Morning and late afternoon usually give softer light than midday.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps painted with team logos outside the dome (it's worth a quick look at the map to confirm where they are), then sit on them with the dome behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it so more of the roof squeezes in over your shoulder. For a different view, the grass slopes at Hitsujigaoka Observation Hill run down toward the dome, so you can stand on the green with the dome far behind you when the grass isn't snow-covered.
card.rules_and_safety: Access around the stadium may be limited on event days, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the roof's curve lines up perfectly with a grid line, then one where you look like you're holding the dome up.
card.good_to_know: Sapporo Dome was designed by Hiroshi Hara and finished in March 2001. It hosted three first-round matches of the 2002 FIFA World Cup. You may see two names on signs, Sapporo Dome or Daiwa House Premist Dome, and the grass football pitch slides in and out of the building when needed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk about 10 minutes from Fukuzumi Station to Sapporo Dome, then stand on the open ground just outside the building, as near the phone icon on the map as you can get. Face the dome so the silver roof fills the frame behind you or your subject.

selfie_spots.why: A visitor sits on these logo-painted steps in a published guide, so the dome serves as the backdrop beyond the usual front view.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole dome in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. The steps-with-team-logos location is inferred to be on the dome grounds from the guide's wording ('in and around the dome'); check it on a map before using it. The Hitsujigaoka grass-slope view comes from a guide that is about 6.5 years old. The Hitsujigaoka statue of Clark is also a selfie spot (a LiveJapan page describes visitors copying its raised-arm pose), but the dome is not behind it, so I left it out. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules or a safety point. The guide's source is cited by title and URL only, as required by the format.

card.hook: Picture a brewery that swapped its beer tanks for shops but kept all the good red brick. That's Sapporo Factory, and the brick side is where your photos are.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in the courtyard in front of the red-brick Renga-kan on the west side of the complex. Face the old brick facade with its greenery; the middle of the complex lies to the north-east behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the brick facade, the greenery and the chimney in one go. Then switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look at the brick wall, and try 2x for close-ups of the ivy or the brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade with the vertical lines so the walls look straight, with the chimney on one third of the frame.
card.best_time: Autumn is the star season, when the ivy on the brick wall turns red. One blogger expected the peak in early November, but it changes from year to year. Summer is fun too, as open beer gardens are often set up in front of the Renga-kan.
card.selfie_here: Head to the square beside the Renga-kan and turn your back to the tall black 'Sapporo Beer' chimney. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the chimney tower over your shoulder. If it's raining, the central atrium under the glass roof, among the indoor plants, is a bright backup.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the same square beside the chimney while you stand in front of the red-brick Renga-kan, so they can fit you, the facade, the chimney and the entrance in one shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The courtyard is an outdoor area within a shopping complex, and shop and event hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the brick facade, the ivy and the chimney all in one frame, with the chimney sitting neatly on a third line?
card.good_to_know: The brewery was built in 1876 for the Kaitakushi, the old Hokkaidō government. It started as a wooden building and was later enlarged in red brick as Sapporo beer became known across Japan. Brewing moved out to Eniwa in 1993, and the buildings were then renovated into the shopping complex you see today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in the courtyard in front of the red-brick Renga-kan on the west side of the complex. Face the old brick facade with its greenery; the middle of the complex lies to the north-east behind you.

selfie_spots.name: Central atrium beneath the glass roof, by the indoor garden
selfie_spots.detail: Stand among the indoor plantings under the glass roof of the central atrium, with the garden and atrium structure behind you.
selfie_spots.why: Sources single out the atrium's glass ceiling, plants and benches as the most photogenic interior setting, and one guide says to get a photo there with the indoor garden.

selfie_research.notes: No fetched page states selfie stick or tripod rules for Sapporo Factory, so none are reported. The ask-someone spot is my inference from the square and the red brick building named in the sources; no page gives a photographer's vantage point for the whole complex, so check it on site. Do not confuse Sapporo Factory's Renga-kan with the separate Former Hokkaido Government Office (Akarenga), which the sources describe as a different landmark. The Trip To Japan and Trip.com pages mention a red brick facade and seasonal decorations but do not name a precise spot.
